specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between unbalanced force, mass and acceleration: force = mass × acceleration F = m × a

primer.text: A book on a desk and a tug-of-war rope tell one story in two halves: sometimes the forces cancel, sometimes they leave a surplus. This note names the two cases, then turns the surplus into the most used equation in mechanics — force equals mass times acceleration.

lessons.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
lessons.opening: Forces on one object combine along each line into a single resultant. When that resultant is zero the forces are balanced and nothing about the motion changes; when a surplus survives, the forces are unbalanced and the object must accelerate. This lesson fixes both words with the two standard scenes.
keyPoints: Balanced forces cancel completely, so the resultant force on the body is zero.
A book on a desk shows the standard balance: its weight downward against the desk's upward push.
Unbalanced forces leave a resultant, and that resultant causes the object to accelerate.
The acceleration may show as speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.
A tug-of-war with 80 N against 100 N leaves a 20 N resultant towards the stronger side.

low.restatement: Cancel completely — balanced, nothing changes. Leave a surplus — unbalanced, and the surplus accelerates the object.
low.analogy: Two shopkeepers haggling over one till: equal pulls hold the till still; the stronger pull walks away with it.
low.examPointer: 'Balanced' questions want the phrase 'resultant force is zero' — not merely 'the forces are equal'.

medium.restatement: Balance is a statement about the resultant, not about stillness: a balanced object keeps whatever velocity it had, while any non-zero resultant rewrites that velocity.
medium.analogy: A barge in steady current: matched tow ropes hold its heading; one extra metre of rope on a side swings it — velocity responds to the surplus, not to the pull.
medium.examPointer: Direction of the acceleration follows the resultant's direction — state both when a question asks for the motion.

check.stem: A book's weight is 12 N downward and the desk pushes up with 12 N. The resultant force on the book is:

options.explanation: The forces oppose; they do not stack.
That is one force alone, not the combination.
Equal opposites cancel to a zero resultant.

options.text: Impossible to say without the mass
options.explanation: The two values already decide the resultant.

check.stem: In a tug-of-war, person A pulls 80 N left and person B pulls 100 N right. The rope's resultant is:

options.explanation: Opposing pulls subtract rather than add.
100 − 80 = 20 N, on the stronger side.
The leftward pull is the weaker one.
Averaging is not the combining law.

check.stem: An unbalanced resultant force must cause the object to:

options.explanation: That is the balanced case.
Constant velocity needs zero resultant.
Mass is untouched by forces.
A non-zero resultant always changes the velocity: speed, direction, or both.

check.stem: Which pair of forces is balanced?

options.explanation: Equal opposites cancel exactly.
A 2 N surplus survives.
Those are not along one line and do not cancel.
Same-direction forces add to 8 N.

check.stem: A crate already sliding at 4 m/s experiences balanced forces. Its motion becomes:

options.text: A stop, because balanced means stationary
options.explanation: Balanced does not mean stationary; it means no change.

options.text: A steady 4 m/s in a straight line
options.explanation: Zero resultant leaves the existing velocity untouched.
Speeding up needs a resultant along the motion.
Turning needs a sideways resultant.

check.stem: State what 'balanced forces' means for the resultant force.
check.modelAnswer: The forces cancel completely, so the resultant force on the body is zero.

check.stem: Name the two forces that balance for a book resting on a desk.
check.modelAnswer: The book's weight acting downward and the desk's upward push on it.

check.stem: Explain why the tug-of-war rope accelerates towards person B when A pulls 80 N and B pulls 100 N.
check.modelAnswer: The two pulls do not cancel: subtracting 80 N from 100 N leaves a 20 N resultant pointing towards B. Any unbalanced force accelerates the body in the resultant's own direction, so the rope gains velocity towards B.

check.stem: Two horizontal pushes act on a crate: 25 N to the right and 10 N to the left. State the resultant and the effect on the crate's motion.
check.modelAnswer: 25 N − 10 N = 15 N to the right; the crate accelerates in that direction, its velocity changing accordingly.

lessons.title: The relationship F = m × a
lessons.opening: One equation runs this whole note: the resultant force equals the mass times the acceleration. This lesson fixes the equation, its units, and the proportionality habits it rewards — doubling force doubles acceleration, doubling mass halves it — then applies all three in worked numbers.
keyPoints: The relationship is force = mass × acceleration, written F = m × a, also known as Newton's second law.
F is the resultant force in newtons, m the mass in kilograms, a the acceleration in metres per second squared.
For a fixed mass, doubling the resultant force doubles the acceleration.
For a fixed force, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
A negative F value records a force acting opposite to the motion — a decelerating force.

low.restatement: Push harder on the same mass and it speeds up faster; push the same on a heavier mass and it speeds up more slowly.
low.analogy: Supermarket trolleys: an empty trolley leaps away at the same shove; the half-full one needs double the shove for the same getaway.
low.examPointer: Always check the units before substituting: kilograms and metres per second squared feed newtons directly.

medium.restatement: F = m × a is a proportionality law, not just a formula: a scales with F for fixed m and with 1/m for fixed F — the two habits behind most rearrangement questions.
medium.analogy: It behaves like a see-saw: force and mass at the ends, acceleration the tilt — load one end double and the tilt answers in kind.
medium.examPointer: When a question hands you a negative force, say why: the minus sign marks a force opposing the motion, exactly the crash-test deceleration case.

check.stem: In F = m × a, the resultant force is measured in:

options.explanation: Kilograms measure the mass.
Force's unit is the newton (N).
That is a velocity unit.
That is the acceleration's unit.

check.stem: A 4 kg trolley is pushed by a 12 N resultant force. Its acceleration is:

options.explanation: That multiplies instead of dividing.
That divides the wrong way.
That adds the two values.

check.stem: The same resultant force acts on a trolley whose mass is then doubled. The new acceleration is:

options.explanation: Mass sits in the denominator; it cannot leave a unchanged.
That is the force habit, not the mass habit.
A non-zero force on any mass gives non-zero acceleration.
Doubling m halves a for the same F.

check.stem: A crash calculation returns F = −14000 N for a passenger. The minus sign records that:

options.explanation: The sign is meaningful, not erroneous.
Masses never enter with a minus here.

options.text: The force acts opposite to the passenger's motion
options.explanation: The decelerating force opposes the travel — that is what the minus encodes.
Squaring has no place in the law.

check.stem: A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 18 m/s in 6 s. The resultant force is:

options.explanation: That divides mass by time — not the law.
That multiplies mass by the final velocity.
That double-counts the time.

check.stem: Write the equation linking unbalanced force, mass and acceleration, with the unit of each quantity.
check.modelAnswer: F = m × a: force in newtons, mass in kilograms, acceleration in metres per second squared.

check.stem: Under which famous name is F = m × a also known?
Explain why the decelerating force on a crash-test passenger carries a minus sign.
check.modelAnswer: The force points opposite to the passenger's motion. The minus sign records that opposing direction — which is exactly why the force slows the passenger to a halt instead of speeding them up.

check.stem: A 70 kg passenger travelling at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 0.1 s. Calculate the deceleration and the force on the passenger.
check.modelAnswer: a = (0 − 20)/0.1 = −200 m/s², and F = 70 × (−200) = −14000 N — the minus showing the force opposes the motion.

glossary.definition: Describes forces whose combination leaves a non-zero resultant on the body.
The unit of force: 1 N accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s².
The rate of change of velocity, in metres per second squared.
The law that the resultant force equals mass times acceleration, F = m × a.

workedExample.prompt: A car of mass 900 kg accelerates from rest to 27 m/s in 3 s. Calculate (a) the acceleration and (b) the force producing it.
steps: List the known quantities: initial velocity 0 m/s, final velocity 27 m/s, time 3 s, mass 900 kg.
The acceleration is the velocity change over time: a = (27 − 0)/3.
Newton's second law then gives F = m × a = 900 × 9.
